prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B033) as the sole prize part with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer, and my configuration has not changed since round 1. Having read the full exchange, the case holds on the criteria I apply as an experimentalist: a quantitative, falsifiable prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011); a decisive measurement at the predicted angle (Jarillo-Herrero's group, 2018); independent reproduction by many groups across graphene multilayers and other moire systems; and a tunable control knob that opens a regime of correlated matter that was not accessible before. Six of eight members now name the same trio, but I do not rest on that count. The convergence matters only because it comes from several independent lines of argument that I find sound. The citation should be narrow: it honours the prediction and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, and does not claim to explain the pairing mechanism or to date the whole moire field from 2018.
statement.case_against: The weak points are the third seat and maturity. Andrei's pre-2018 STM and transport work is a real earlier experimental strand, and the first authors of the 2018 papers and the Dean and Kim hBN device work are left outside a three-person split. As a non-specialist in condensed matter I cannot adjudicate the priority question myself, and the colleagues who can have given a consistent but not unanimous reading: Andrei showed flat-band-like features and Van Hove singularities, whereas the correlated and superconducting phases that define the discovery appeared in the 2018 work. The pairing mechanism is open and sample-to-sample twist-angle disorder is a real limit on how sharply the experimental claims can be stated. I accept that this is the least mature of the strong candidates in its theory, though not in its phenomenology. If a condensed-matter colleague can show that Andrei's work established the flat-band prediction experimentally in a way that is comparable to the 2018 result, I would change the third name. So far the committee has not shown that.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from Andrei to Bistritzer for the third seat but keeps it as the weakest part of the configuration, and says Cao as first author raises a question about crediting the group leader under the three-person rule.
responses.response: I asked you in round 1 for a priority judgement and your answer is useful: Andrei's STM work established localisation and Van Hove singularities, but the prediction is the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper and the correlated phases came in 2018. I accept that reasoning and have kept Bistritzer in the third seat. On Cao I agree with you that the statutes force a choice and that the leader of the experimental programme is a defensible credit, but the discussion record should say so explicitly, and I would not want the citation to read as though the junior authors contributed nothing. I also take your point that continuum-model flat bands are an idealisation once relaxation and strain matter. That is a reason to word the citation around the prediction of the magic angle and the observed phases, not around a settled microscopic theory.

responses.point: Kroll holds B026 as lead but offers B033 as his first alternative, and argues that twist-angle disorder makes the experimental credit harder to pin down than a clock comparison where independent labs agree at 1e-18.
responses.response: This is the sharpest objection to B033 and I give it real weight, since it is the test I apply myself. The comparison is fair but the standards are not identical, because the things being confirmed are different. For clocks it is a number, which different labs can agree on to many digits. For twisted bilayer graphene it is the existence of a phase diagram with correlated insulators and superconducting domes at the magic angle, and that has been reproduced by many groups, with the sample dependence affecting the details and the quantitative location of features and not the existence of the phases. I would apply one common standard to both: independent groups, using independent devices or apparatus, find the claimed effect. B026 meets that standard by a wider margin on precision, B033 meets it on the question that the citation actually asks. I have not changed my ranking over this, but I agree your point should be recorded in the discussion.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that lattice clocks solve a distinct problem, keeping the stability benefit of many atoms without perturbing the transition, so they are a new idea and not a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and says the pending redefinition of the second should not be cited as a reason for timing.
responses.response: You have moved me on both points. On novelty, your distinction between the comb as a ruler, the single-ion control prize, and a many-atom lattice that cancels light shifts is a convincing reason to treat B026 as a separate achievement, and I withdraw my round-1 suggestion that the earlier prizes make it look incremental. On timing I agree that a prize should rest on what has been demonstrated and cross-checked and not on a metrology decision that has not been taken. That makes B026 the stronger of my alternatives and the natural candidate for a later year, with the clean Katori and Ye credit. I still prefer B033 this year because of the breadth of new physics it opens, but that is a judgement about what to reward first, and I do not think it makes your case weak.

responses.point: Danielsson supports B033 and says recognising the platform before the pairing mechanism is understood may look premature in hindsight, and wants the committee to see whether the discovery is the platform or a settled explanation.
responses.response: I think the right answer is that we are honouring the platform and the phase diagram, not an explanation, and that the citation should say so. Our own history supports this: we have recognised experimental discoveries whose mechanism was incomplete, and the discovery in that case is what experiments established and others reproduced. Where I would go further than you is the case for waiting a few years. Waiting would help to settle the third seat if new evidence comes in, but I do not see any scientific question that is likely to remove the flat-band prediction or the correlated phases, so I would not postpone on maturity grounds alone.

uncertainties: Whether the committee has given Andrei's pre-2018 work the examination it needs. My condensed-matter judgement rests on colleagues' readings of scope and dating, which I cannot verify here.
Whether leaving out the first authors of the 2018 papers and the Dean and Kim device work can be defended publicly under the three-person limit, even with a narrow citation.
How much weight the open pairing mechanism and device-to-device variation should carry, given that I would apply the same independent-confirmation standard to B033 and B026.
If B033 fails on credit, whether B026 is the better fallback than B009, where the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang prediction and the Mele versus Hasan question are still unresolved.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my earlier disclosure. I have no collaboration or institutional tie to any credited name on B033, B026 or B009. I disclose that my own field of astroparticle physics overlaps with IceCube (B024), my opening first choice, with no collaboration and no current proposal of it, and that my judgements on condensed-matter and atomic-physics candidates depend on colleagues. As Chair I try not to let my process role weigh in favour of any candidate.
